<!--Temporal patterns of outdegree (\gls{dco}) characteristics in Figure \ref{fig:sectpnda}(a) and the \gls{ec} in Figure \ref{fig:sectpnda}(e), which refers to the export partners (\gls{dco}) and the embeddedness (\gls{ec}), can be classified into two groups. Until the 2008 financial crisis, these two clusters essentially moved together, while after 2008 the trend of the two clusters diverged. The first cluster, which includes agricultural products, mining support activities, food products, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, mechanical and motor vehicle equipment, warehousing and postal services, accommodation, IT, publishing, scientific activities, administrative activities, public sector, social work and the arts, continues to strengthen after the crisis, albeit at a slower pace compared to the pre-crisis period. Until then, the second group of industries (such as mining, textile products, wood, paper and oil products, basic metals, transport equipment, electrical machinery, water and waste management, construction, air transport, telecommunications, education, and other activities) stagnates after the financial crisis. According to forecasts, both industries will expand the number of export partners.

Homophily in Figure \ref{fig:sectpnda}(b), which shows the percentage of import and export partners from a given sector compared to all partners, decreases slightly for both clusters. The sectors of the two clusters overlap greatly with the groups clustered based on the growth of export partners (compare Figures Figure \ref{fig:sectpnda}(a) and (b)). The second group has significantly lower homophily value. According to forecasts, the homophily value of the industries in the first group will decrease, while the other two are expected to stagnate between 2021-2030.

Modularity in Figure \ref{fig:sectpnda}(c) indicates the concentration of relationships by industry groups. The applied \gls{gnda} method identifies 3 industry clusters. The modularity value of the first cluster decreases between 1995-2015 from 0.76 to 0.63, where it stagnates thereafter. This cluster includes agriculture, hunting and forestry, non-energy mining, food industry, wood and metal equipment, computer and manufacturing equipment, electrical and mechanical equipment, water transport. The industries belonging to the second cluster, fishing, mining auxiliary equipment, refined oil, motor vehicles, various means of transport, accommodation, publishing and broadcasting, financial and insurance services, scientific and technical services, education, social work, arts, whose module rate fluctuates. It decreases slightly (2.5%) from 1995 to 2002, then increases between 2003 and 2012 (7.5%), and then decreases again until 2015. In contrast, the third industry group, which includes energy extraction, waste management, postal services, administrative and support services, public utilities and defense, stagnated at a high level (0.78-0.80) between 1995 and 2010, while after 2010, the concentration decreased by about 5% over the 10 years. Also in this case, according to forecasts, the modularity of the industries in the first group will decrease, while the other two are expected to stagnate between 2021-2030.

In Figure \ref{fig:sectpnda}(e-f), we can identify three different industry groups based on both \gls{prc} and \gls{bc} values. The \gls{prc} centrality of all industry groups has stagnated over time, except for the financial crisis of 2008. The industries in the first group have the highest centrality, which includes, among others, non-energy mining, food industry, paper and metal products, all forms of transport, scientific and administrative activities. The \gls{prc} value is similarly high for the agricultural industry, energy mining, postal services, and the financial and defense. The last, lowest \gls{prc} value is for the pharmaceutical industry, warehousing, and the arts. While we know how much the importance of the first two industries in particular has increased during the pandemic. The value of \gls{bc} in Figure  \ref{fig:sectpnda}(f) decreases for the industries in the first group. The first group includes, among others, agricultural industry, fishing, electrical industry, retail and wholesale trade, construction, and all transport industries. These industries had the largest intermediary role, but they gradually lost this role every year and, according to forecasts, a further decrease is expected between 2021-2030. The second group, whose intermediary role is increasing slightly, includes mining, rubber and plastics products, basic metals, installation of machinery and equipment, postal and courier activities, publishing, audiovisual and broadcasting activities, telecommunications, IT and other information services. The lowest and at the same time relatively constant \gls{bc} are found in wood and products of wood and cork, computer, electronic and optical equipment, motor vehicles, real estate activities, public administration and defense, and the education.-->

The final results of the causality analysis are shown in Figure \ref{fig:caussect}. This calculation follows the steps of causality analysis on network-level indicators; see Figure \ref{fig:causnetwp}. First, the Granger and instantaneous causalities are calculated. Causality graphs are specified and aligned as a tree layout. Each level of trees is grouped into a block, and the average time lag between the pair of elements from a two distinct blocks is calculated.

```{r caussect,echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE,fig.align='center',fig.cap="Industrial effect mechanisms based on causality and cluster analysis with economic interpretation of sectoral groupings",fig.subcap=c("Outdegree centrality, homophily, modularity","Eigenvector centrality, PageRank Centrality, Betweenness Centrality"),fig.ncol=2,out.width = '48%',fig.pos="H",results='hide',fig.asp=0.62}

#fig.subcap=c("Granger causality on degree centralities","Instantaneous causality on degree centralities","Granger causality on homophylies","Instantaneous causality on homophylies","Granger causality on Leiden's modularity","Instantaneous causality on Leiden's modularity","Precedences of sectors"),
# DCO

var_sect_time_mean<-apply(var_sect_country_time[,,1:77,] , c(1,2,4), FUN=mean) 


sectdata<-as.data.frame(t(var_sect_time[3,,]))
N<-ncol(sectdata)
p<-0.01
FILENAME<-"data/CAUS_SECT_DCO.RData"
FILEEXISTS<-file.exists(FILENAME)
if (FILEEXISTS==TRUE){
  load(FILENAME)
}else{
  INSTANT_SECT<-GRANGER_SECT<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,nrow = N,ncol = N))
  rownames(INSTANT_SECT)<-rownames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(INSTANT_SECT)<-colnames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(sectdata)
  for (i in 1:N){
    for (j in 1:N){
      if (i != j){
        ts1<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,i])),start=1995,end=2020)
        ts2<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,j])),start=1995,end=2020)
        tsDat<-ts.union(ts1,ts2)
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_g<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Granger$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_g)) {p_g<-1}
          if (p_g<p){
            if (bayesian_granger_causality(ts1,ts2,k)$
                bayes_factor>10){
              GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-k
              break
            }
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_i<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Instant$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_i)) {p_i<-1}
          if (p_i<p){
            INSTANT_SECT[i,j]<-1
            GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-0
            break
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        
      }
    }
  }
  
  save(GRANGER_SECT,INSTANT_SECT,file = FILENAME)
}

            break
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }

# MODULARITY

sectdata<-as.data.frame(t(var_sect_time[13,,]))
N<-ncol(sectdata)
p<-0.01
FILENAME<-"data/CAUS_SECT_MODU.RData"
FILEEXISTS<-file.exists(FILENAME)
if (FILEEXISTS==TRUE){
  load(FILENAME)
}else{
  INSTANT_SECT<-GRANGER_SECT<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,nrow = N,ncol = N))
  rownames(INSTANT_SECT)<-rownames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(INSTANT_SECT)<-colnames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(sectdata)
  for (i in 1:N){
    for (j in 1:N){
      if (i != j){
        ts1<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,i])),start=1995,end=2020)
        ts2<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,j])),start=1995,end=2020)
        tsDat<-ts.union(ts1,ts2)
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_g<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Granger$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_g)) {p_g<-1}
          if (p_g<p){
            if (bayesian_granger_causality(ts1,ts2,k)$
                bayes_factor>10){
              GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-k
              break
            }
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_i<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Instant$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_i)) {p_i<-1}
          if (p_i<p){
            INSTANT_SECT[i,j]<-1
            GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-0
            break
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        
      }
    }
  }
  
  save(GRANGER_SECT,INSTANT_SECT,file = FILENAME)
}

if (FILEEXISTS==TRUE){
  load(FILENAME)
}else{
  INSTANT_SECT<-GRANGER_SECT<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,nrow = N,ncol = N))
  rownames(INSTANT_SECT)<-rownames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(INSTANT_SECT)<-colnames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(sectdata)
  for (i in 1:N){
    for (j in 1:N){
      if (i != j){
        ts1<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,i])),start=1995,end=2020)
        ts2<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,j])),start=1995,end=2020)
        tsDat<-ts.union(ts1,ts2)
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_g<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Granger$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_g)) {p_g<-1}
          if (p_g<p){
            if (bayesian_granger_causality(ts1,ts2,k)$
                bayes_factor>10){
              GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-k
              break
            }
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_i<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Instant$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_i)) {p_i<-1}
          if (p_i<p){
            INSTANT_SECT[i,j]<-1
            GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-0
            break
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        
      }
    }
  }
  
  save(GRANGER_SECT,INSTANT_SECT,file = FILENAME)
}

# PRC

sectdata<-as.data.frame(t(var_sect_time_mean[23,,]))
N<-ncol(sectdata)
p<-0.01
FILENAME<-"data/CAUS_SECT_PRC.RData"
FILEEXISTS<-file.exists(FILENAME)
if (FILEEXISTS==TRUE){
  load(FILENAME)
}else{
  INSTANT_SECT<-GRANGER_SECT<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,nrow = N,ncol = N))
  rownames(INSTANT_SECT)<-rownames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(INSTANT_SECT)<-colnames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(sectdata)
  for (i in 1:N){
    for (j in 1:N){
      if (i != j){
        ts1<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,i])),start=1995,end=2020)
        ts2<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,j])),start=1995,end=2020)
        tsDat<-ts.union(ts1,ts2)
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_g<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Granger$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_g)) {p_g<-1}
          if (p_g<p){
            if (bayesian_granger_causality(ts1,ts2,k)$
                bayes_factor>10){
              GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-k
              break
            }
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_i<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Instant$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_i)) {p_i<-1}
          if (p_i<p){
            INSTANT_SECT[i,j]<-1
            GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-0
            break
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        
      }
    }
  }
  
  save(GRANGER_SECT,INSTANT_SECT,file = FILENAME)
}

if (FILEEXISTS==TRUE){
  load(FILENAME)
}else{
  INSTANT_SECT<-GRANGER_SECT<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,nrow = N,ncol = N))
  rownames(INSTANT_SECT)<-rownames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(INSTANT_SECT)<-colnames(GRANGER_SECT)<-colnames(sectdata)
  for (i in 1:N){
    for (j in 1:N){
      if (i != j){
        ts1<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,i])),start=1995,end=2020)
        ts2<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(sectdata[,j])),start=1995,end=2020)
        tsDat<-ts.union(ts1,ts2)
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_g<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Granger$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_g)) {p_g<-1}
          if (p_g<p){
            if (bayesian_granger_causality(ts1,ts2,k)$
                bayes_factor>10){
              GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-k
              break
            }

          if (k>4){
            break

          k<-k+1

        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_i<-as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Instant$p.value)
          if (is.na(p_i)) {p_i<-1}
          if (p_i<p){
            INSTANT_SECT[i,j]<-1
            GRANGER_SECT[i,j]<-0
            break
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        
      }
    }
  }
  
  save(GRANGER_SECT,INSTANT_SECT,file = FILENAME)
}

<!--Figure \ref{fig:caussect}  identifies the industries where signs of structural change first appear. These include, in the area of export relations, agricluture and food industries, paper and printed products, chemicals, finished metal products, computing, electronic and optical equipment, land and pipeline transport, warehousing, postal services, IT services, scientific and technical services. This is followed by fishing, non-energy mining, refined petroleum, electricity, gas, water, accommodation, finance and insurance, education, arts, with an average lag of 1.73 years, followed by maintenance, woodworking, medicine, electrical products, construction, water and air transport, telecommunications, public sector and the defense sector with an average lag of 3.04 years. Here, a backlash with an average lag of 1.58 years can be observed. The last sector is energy mining.

In the case of analyzing the presdences of homophily of industries, signifying organizational change, are seen in the computer, electrical, optical, and accommodation sectors.  Subsequently, energy mining, paper and printing, fabricated metal goods, electronic equipment, building, postal services, education, social work, and the arts exhibit an average delay of 3.4 years.  Agriculture and food sector, non-energy mining, medical equipment, electricity, gas, water services, publishing, broadcasting, information technology, telecommunications, finance, insurance, public services, and defense, each exhibiting an average delay of 2.67 years.  Additionally, there is a backlash with an average delay of 2.12 years.  The sectors classified under the fourth group -- refined oil, medical equipment, waste management, water transport, warehousing, administrative activities, the automobile industry, and ancillary services -- exhibit the most significant fluctuations. Postponed consequences are also evident in the final three industrial groupings.

The alteration in modularity that defines fragmentation is initially experienced in land transportation.  It manifests after an average duration of 2.06 years within the electrical equipment, machinery, fishing, broadcasting, financial activities, science, and art sectors. The fragmentation transition occurs after an average of 2.48 years in the agriculture and food business, completed products, and IT and information services. The extraction of energy resources, aviation, public services, and defense industries exhibit an average delay of 3.44 years.  In every instance, these industry groups also influence the preceding groups.

In terms of eigenvector centralities, most sectors move together. However, changes first appear in the areas of public service and defense, and human health and social works. This is followed by accommodation, arts, entertainment and recreation, air transport and the Textiles, textile products, leather and footwear industries with an average delay of 1.25 years. Changes in PageRank and Betweenness centralities first appear in the water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (E) industries. On average, after 2.36 years, the PageRank centrality of minings (B05-B09), basic metals,   computer, electronic and equipments, wholesale and retail trade, acommodation, publishing, telecommunication financial and insurance, administrative and support service industries also changes. And on average 2.77 years later, agriculture, fishing, textiles, woods, paper products, electrical and machinery equipment, trasports, scientific publishing and education. After 2.64 non metalic product, fabricated materials, construction, IT, public administration and arts. While the lastly changed industry in the PageRank Centrality is the rubber and plastic products. 

In the case of betweenness centrality after changing water supply; sewerage, waste industry, changes appear four years later in the fabricated metal products and air transport industries. This is followed by mining and quarrying, non-energy, with a delay of 2.81 years producing products, coke and refined petroleum products (C19), chemical products, pharmaceuticals, Rubber and plastics products, basic metals, computer, electronic and optical equipment, wholesale and retail trade, water transport, IT, real estates, arts, entertainment and recreation, and education. This is followed by 2.22 years later, including the electronics industry, construction, land transport, postal and courier activities, financial and insurance activities, professional, scientific and technical activities. Betweenness centrality changes at the latest in the agriculture, hunting, forestry, fishing and aquaculture, warehousing and support activities for transportation sectors.-->

## Country-Level Analysis

Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry} shows the top ten countries with the greatest centrality values. The \gls{sco} in Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(a) actually shows the volume of exports considering the ten largest exporters, whereas Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(c) shows the trade balance \gls{sco}-\gls{sci}=export-import in time. Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(b, d-g) shows the ten most important countries with the largest relative PageRank, hub, authority, betweenness and eigenvector centrality values, where the relative centrality value of a given country is calculated by dividing the summed centrality values of all industries of that country by the sum of the centrality values of all industries of all countries. In this way, the sum of the relative centrality values of the top ten countries with the greatest values indicate their role compared to that of all other countries. The change in values over time gives the change in the relative position of the top ten countries. To control the changes in centralities we calculate the changes in \glspl{fd} (see Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(h)).

<!--Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(a) illustrates the primary exporting nations.  The results indicate that the export volume of the top 10 nations experienced a modest growth from 1995 to 2002, followed by a substantial rise from 2002 to 2008.  The 2008 financial crisis interrupted export performance, which experienced a moderate increase until 2016, followed by fluctuations and subsequent stagnation prior to the COVID pandemic.  China saw a lesser impact from the financial crisis.  China successfully augmented export volumes across all sectors.  The ascent of China is illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(b), which depicts the distribution of PageRank centrality among the top 10 nations from 1995 to 2020.  The ten principal countries experienced a marginal gain in their overall impact; however, with the exception of China, the relative PageRank centrality values of the remaining nine countries diminished, whereas China's value rose.  Upon examining the balance of exports and imports in Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(c), which represents the \gls{sco}-\gls{sci} in terms of centralities, it is evident that China's import demand has escalated beyond its export performance.  The distributions of hub (Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(d)) and authority centrality (Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(e)) exhibit a similar trend.  The ten highlighted countries possess approximately 100% of the centralities.  The transformation of the roles of China and the United States is remarkable; the United States dominated these centralities until 2012, after which China abruptly assumed the role and effectively retained its position until 2020, with the exception of 2017.  These centralities also consider the centrality of its suppliers and customers.  The rise in centralities indicates that China is deliberately seeking to enhance its standing not only in commerce but also by focusing on all aspects of the supply chain, aiming to become a predominant force in several industries.  The alteration of trade relations is further illustrated by the reconfiguration of \gls{bc} in Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(f).  China is fortifying its position relative to the other nine largest nations.  China's fortification in this context signifies not only the enhancement of its intermediary function but also its increasingly indispensable role in supply chains (see Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(d-e)).  The results are partly influenced by the collective 10% decrease in the \gls{ec} of the top 10 nations (see Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(f)).  A minor gain is noted in China; however, this does not offset the decline in the relative centrality of other nations.-->

Figure \ref{fig:ctryaggr} shows the impact mechanism of changes in all trade activities (import+export with \gls{sc}) measured. The map shows OECD countries. The size of the nodes is proportional to the total trade activity (imports + exports), which is measured via strength centrality. The colors of the nodes indicate the causal group into which each country falls. The first causal relationship is for countries whose trade changes first. The last causal relationship is for countries whose trade changes last. By biclustering the causal relations, one significant group of relationships can be identified, which are indicated by the colors of the arrows.

p<-0.01
FILENAME<-"data/CAUS_CTRY_SC.RData"
FILEEXISTS<-file.exists(FILENAME)
if (FILEEXISTS==TRUE){
  load(FILENAME)
}else{
  GRANGER_CTRY<-INSTANT_CTRY<-as.data.frame(matrix(0,nrow=length(countries),ncol=length(countries)))
  colnames(GRANGER_CTRY)<-rownames(GRANGER_CTRY)<-colnames(INSTANT_CTRY)<-rownames(INSTANT_CTRY)<-countries
  for (i in 1:nrow(D3_data)){
    for (j in 1:nrow(D3_data)){
      ts1Name=rownames(D3_data)[i]
      ts2Name=rownames(D3_data)[j]
      if (ts1Name!=ts2Name){
        ts1<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(D3_data[i,])),start=1995,end=2020)
        ts2<-ts(as.numeric(as.matrix(D3_data[j,])),start=1995,end=2020)
        tsDat<-ts.union(ts1,ts2)
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_g<-try(as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Granger$p.value),silent = TRUE)
          if (!is(p_g,"numeric")) {p_g<-1}
          if (is.na(p_g)) {p_g<-1}
          if (p_g<p){
            if (bayesian_granger_causality(ts1,ts2,k)$
                bayes_factor>10){  GRANGER_CTRY[ts1Name,ts2Name]<-k
                break
            }
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
        k<-1
        while (TRUE)
        {
          tsVAR <- vars::VAR(tsDat, p = k)
          p_i<-try(as.numeric(causality(tsVAR, cause = "ts1")$Instant$p.value),silent = TRUE)
          if (!is(p_i,"numeric")) {p_i<-1}
          if (is.na(p_i)) {p_i<-1}
          if (p_i<p){
            INSTANT_CTRY[ts1Name,ts2Name]<-1
            GRANGER_CTRY[ts1Name,ts2Name]<-0
            break
          }
          if (k>4){
            break
          }
          k<-k+1
        }
      }
    }
  }
  save(GRANGER_CTRY,INSTANT_CTRY,file = FILENAME)
}

Figure \ref{fig:ctryaggr} maps the temporal propagation of trade volume, which changes across 77 countries from 1995-2020, revealing systematic patterns in how global trade disruptions cascade through different national economies. Figure \ref{fig:ctryaggr} (a) presents the clustered Granger causality network where nodes represent country size proportionally to total trade activity (imports + exports measured by strength centrality), and node colors indicate causal group membership based on response timing. Dark red arrows represent significant causal relationships (bicluster 1) where changes in one country's trade volume predict changes in another with specific time lags, while light green arrows show nonsignificant relationships (bicluster 2). Figure \ref{fig:ctryaggr} (b) synthesizes the effect mechanism into four hierarchical tiers with distinct economic characteristics. Figure \ref{fig:ctryaggr} shows that the change in trade occurs simultaneously in most countries. Such changes can be divided into four consecutive causal groups in time. Trade changes first appear in `r toString(country_LUT_SP$Country[country_LUT_SP$Code %in% levels[[1]]])`. Afterward, at average, in `r year12` years, the larger set of trade countries is `r toString(country_LUT_SP$Country[country_LUT_SP$Code %in% levels[[2]]])`. A change in a larger group of countries can also be observed, on average, `r year23` years later, such as `r toString(country_LUT_SP$Country[country_LUT_SP$Code %in% levels[[3]]])`. A backlash can also be observed between the two middle groups with an average delay of `r year32` years. The last group includes a total of `r length(levels[[4]])` countries, namely `r toString(country_LUT_SP$Country[country_LUT_SP$Code %in% levels[[4]]])`, which are those countries where export/import changes in trade appear the latest in the considered period.

# Discussion

## Structural Changes in the Trade Network

<!--In the period examined from 1995 to 2020, several distinct periods emerge in the structural indicators of the dynamic multilayer trade network (see Figure \ref{fig:netwp}). One striking observation is the notable increase in \gls{dzi}, \gls{dzo}, and \gls{bz}, indicating that certain nodes -- representing countries -- are becoming increasingly influential within the network. This centralization reflects a concentration of resources and trade power, where particular players dominate strategic industries, driven by technological advancements and shifts in production patterns. The rise of digital technologies and supply chain optimizations has enabled firms within countries to leverage their network positions more effectively, further enhancing these centralizations. The findings reveal significant improvements in resilience and local and global efficiency and a decreasing average path length, suggesting that the network is becoming more interconnected and efficient over time. These shifts can be attributed to technological advancements that facilitate communication and the flow of goods across borders, thereby enhancing global cooperation. As connectivity increases, the network's density marginally increases, whereas the transition to an increasingly disassortative network reflects a diversification of industries and cross-industry collaborations. This behavior suggests that countries are not only striving to improve their presence across multiple sectors but are also embedding themselves within various industry relationships, facilitating the diffusion of innovation and technology. Interestingly, the parallel rise in \gls{ns} across industries indicates a trend where countries gravitate toward similar industrial roles, aligning their trade strategies in the wake of globalization. In contrast, the emergence of increasingly diversified connection systems within each industry -- evidenced by declining degree similarity -- suggests a shift from homogeneity to heterogeneity in industry networks. This evolution is likely influenced by the shifting dynamics of global trade, with actors such as China playing a pivotal role in reshaping external economic relations. As countries adapt to these trends, the economic landscape continuously evolves, reflecting a blend of competition and collaboration in the pursuit of market efficiency and resilience.

The 2008 financial crisis was not just a temporary setback but also slowed global trends, presenting the difficulties of "slowbalization" -- local or national realities challenging and reshaping global norms and practices [@benabed2024slowbalization]. After the financial crisis, governments prioritized domestic stability and economic recovery through international collaboration and integration, slowing globalization. This protectionist trend led to trade restrictions and the heightened scrutiny of global financial systems, which departed from precrisis interconnected prosperity. An increasingly cautious and selective approach to global markets arose as the world adjusted to the crisis.

For most indicators, 2016 marked another trend reversal. At that time, the emerging US--China tariff war, which has intensified since Donald Trump's inauguration and is entering a new phase in 2025, is breaking the trend again. Most indicators stagnate during this period, and then in 2018, shortly before COVID-19 and the start of the Russia--Ukraine conflict and the associated sanctions, they had already begun to deteriorate.

If trade networks are not subjected to disruptions caused by sanctions from the Russia--Ukraine conflict, supply chain issues post-COVID-19, or protective tariffs from the Trump administration, then the forecasts suggest that several structural indicators will likely show more favorable dynamics. In such a scenario, resilience across the trade network is expected to improve steadily, as these external shocks do not exacerbate vulnerabilities or fragment supply chains further. Without these distortions, resilience values may rebound more robustly, recovering from earlier stagnation, which could lead to more cohesive global trade network, with improved adaptability to smaller-scale disruptions.

The projections for degree centralizations indicate continued growth, which, in the absence of geopolitical and economic shocks, might be less uneven and more stable. Such a dynamic could imply a further concentration of influence among dominant actors, but with a more balanced and gradual evolution. Similarly, transitivity and efficiency, which are forecasted to rise between 2021 and 2030, would likely show enhanced performance due to uninterrupted trade flows and reduced fragmentation. This could foster stronger network cohesiveness and a streamlined global trade structure, enabling smoother interactions and exchanges between countries.

Furthermore, certain indicators, such as modularity and PageRank concentration, would have decreased as predicted, which underscores the inherent shifts in trade networks toward greater interconnectivity and less segmentation. The shortening of average path lengths (AVPLs) and increasing density would likely accelerate, reflecting a continued supply chain shortening and a more interconnected network. These dynamics, unhindered by external shocks, could have enhanced efficiency and reduced trade asymmetries, fostering a more resilient and equitable global trade network in the face of future uncertainties.-->

Concentration and market power. The steady rise of importer and exporter centralization and of intermediation power (degree and betweenness centralizations; PageRank centralization; “rich-club” intensity) signals a persistent concentration of global trade in a relatively small set of hub economies. Economically, this implies growing bargaining power for core countries and lead firms, stronger price-setting capacity along \glspl{gvc}, and a greater potential for policy shocks in a few jurisdictions to transmit widely. The timing is consistent with welldocumented structural drivers: the post-1995 offshoring boom, the 2001 \gls{wto} accession of China, and the scaling of platform-type supply chains. Nonnetwork evidence aligns with this pattern: the “export superstars” phenomenon indicates a concentration of exports in a small share of firms [@freund2015export; @rowley2024domestic], while the “Great Convergence” describes how \gls{ict} lowered coordination costs and enabled hub-and-spoke \glspl{gvc} led by a few economies and firms [@baldwin2016great]. China’s increasing systemic centrality in Figure \ref{fig:netwp} is consistent with macro evidence on the “China shock” and its broad real-economy repercussions [@autor2016china; @dorn2024labour].

Efficiency, trade costs, and chain architecture. The decline in average (multilayer) path lengths and the rise in local and global efficiency indicate economically shorter and more reliable trade routes, consistent with falling trade costs (logistics, coordination, and information) and the maturation of production sharing. This is precisely what one would expect from containerization, \gls{ict} diffusion, and the codification of tasks that enabled fine slicing of value chains [@hummels2001nature; @ren2024regional; @baldwin2016great]. The small but persistent increase in density further reflects broadening market access and deeper integration. Microevidence that “time is trade cost” (e.g., delays at the border and in shipping depress trade disproportionately) provides an independent, nonnetwork rationale for the shorter effective distances we observe [@liu2013investigating]. In economic terms, Figure \ref{fig:netwp} suggests that, up to the mid-2010s, firms optimized to minimize coordination and leadtime risk while leveraging larger supplier networks.

Regionalization vs. global integration. Modularity and assortativity patterns capture the tension between regionalization and global integration. Assortativity trending more negative is consistent with a hub-and-spoke, core-periphery architecture: highly connected hubs transact extensively with less connected periphery nodes -- a hallmark of lead-firm \glspl{gvc}. Modularity dynamics point to an ebb and flow between global integration and the re-emergence of regional blocs. The post-2008 “slowbalization” debate emphasized both cyclical (demand, finance) and structural (policy, technology) drivers of a slower trade elasticity [@constantinescu2020global]. Figure \ref{fig:netwp} is consistent with a period of re-regionalization around the mid-to-late 2010s as trade policy frictions rose [@evenett2019protectionism], even as the underlying technology and logistics fundamentals continued to support efficient cross-border production. Put differently, the economic forces pushing toward integration (falling trade costs) and the policy forces pushing toward fragmentation (tariffs, screening, compliance divergence) coexisted during this period.

Resilience and systemic risk. Improvement in random failure resilience together with the more modest gains (or plateaus) in targeted-attack resilience imply that while the trade system became better at absorbing idiosyncratic disturbances, it remained vulnerable to shocks concentrated on hubs (e.g., a targeted tariff or a chokepoint disruption). This is an economic tradeoff familiar in the supply chain management: efficiency gains from scale and centralization raise exposure to hub-specific risks. The literature on supply chain risk similarly warns that the very forces that made \glspl{gvc} efficient -- supplier consolidation, just-in-time inventories, and hub concentration -- also magnifies systemic vulnerability to policy and logistical shocks [@baldwin2022risks]. The patterns in Figure \ref{fig:netwp} therefore square with an economic interpretation in which firms optimized for cost and speed during “normal times,” while policy shocks and crises reveal the nonlinear losses associated with central-node disruptions.

The counterfactual outlook lacks recent shocks. The ARIMA-based projections (2021–2030) are a baseline, “no-new-shock” counterfactual. Economically, the forecast of continued efficiency gains (shorter effective distances), slight additional densification, and mild declines in modular segmentation suggests that, the absence of new protectionist measures or large geopolitical events, the gravitational pull of technology, scale, and learned coordination would have continued to deepen integration and diffuse influence marginally away from the very top players. This counterfactual complements non-network assessments that attribute much of the post-2016 deceleration to policy and uncertainty rather than to a reversal of the technological and organizational underpinnings of \glspl{gvc} [@constantinescu2020global]. In other words, Figure \ref{fig:netwp}’s forecasts imply that the observed fragmentation of recent years is not inevitable; it is contingent on policy and shock realizations rather than being dictated by economic fundamentals alone [@milberg2024globalization].

<!--Figure \ref{fig:causnetwp} reveals that most structural changes occur instantaneously and collectively and that with analysis of the causal mechanisms, causal relations can be grouped into three consecutive categories. The first group is comprised of structural indicators such as transitivity and global clustering, \emph{robustness} of the network configuration characterized by interconnected trade communities and resilience against systematic disruptions. First, the robustness of trade will change, followed by the indicators of the second group, which is dominated by various centralization indicators and similarity indicators, which refers to changes in \emph{concentration} and \emph{fragmentation}. Finally, the last group contains the further centralization and modularity indicators, as well as assortativity. This group presents the property of involving \emph{trade communities}. These indicators change later and influence the second group over time.

Although these data do not yet include the newest and unfolding crises, the results of causality analyses show that shocks or crises, such as financial disruptions or geopolitical conflicts, often lead to significant structural changes in trade networks. Our results show that in the event of disruptions, the robustness of the network changes first, then concentration and fragmentation, and finally, the network of trade communities.-->

As shown in Figure \ref{fig:causnetwp} most structural changes occur instantaneously and collectively, with causal mechanism analysis organizing these relationships into three consecutive hierarchical groups. These findings align with @baldwin2015supply's observation of "deep integration" in global value chains, where interconnected production networks create simultaneous adjustment patterns across multiple economic dimensions. The first tier comprises structural indicators reflecting network robustness--transitivity, global clustering coefficients, and systematic resilience measures--which change earliest in response to economic disruptions. This pattern mirrors @autor2016china's findings on the "China shock," where initial trade policy changes first affected the structural integrity of manufacturing networks before cascading to other sectors. From an economic policy perspective, this suggests that policymakers should monitor network robustness indicators as early warning signals for broader structural changes, as these measures capture the fundamental stability of trade relationships before concentration or community patterns begin to shift.

The second tier encompasses centralization and similarity indicators, reflecting changes in market concentration and trading partner alignment patterns, which respond with an average lag of `r round(ALLyear12,2)` <!--1.35--> years after robustness changes. This delayed response supports @melitz2003impact's heterogeneous firm trade model, where aggregate trade patterns emerge from firm-level adjustments that take time to manifest in network-wide concentration measures. The third tier includes community structure indicators (modularity and assortativity) with an average lag of `r round(ALLyear23,2)` <!--3.31--> years, representing the longest-term structural adjustments in trading bloc formation and partnership preferences. This temporal sequencing contradicts the immediate adjustment assumptions of standard trade models [@krugman1980scale; @mansouri2022brief] but supports more recent dynamic trade literature emphasizing gradual adjustment processes [@eaton2016trade; @atsebi2024sectoral]. Bidirectional causality between the second and third tiers (with a <!--1.26-->`r round(ALLyear32,2)`-year reverse lag) indicates that community structure changes can also influence concentration patterns, suggesting that trade bloc formation can reshape market power dynamics--a finding consistent with @hofmann2019content's analysis of preferential trade agreements' effects on multilateral trade patterns. These results provide crucial guidance for crisis management: robust early intervention during the first phase can prevent cascading effects, whereas delayed responses may require addressing all three structural dimensions simultaneously at much higher economic and political costs.

The centrality values shown in Figure \ref{fig:top10sect} reveal remarkable structural stability in global trade hierarchies despite major economic disruptions, suggesting that fundamental comparative advantages and industrial specialization patterns exhibit strong persistence over time. The dominance of wholesale and retail trade (G), financial services (K), and basic metals (C24) in export volumes and centrality measures aligns with @hausmann2011network's economic complexity theory, which predicts that countries and industries with established capabilities maintain their positions in global value networks. This stability contradicts the "creative destruction" hypothesis of @schumpeter2013capitalism, which would predict more dramatic industrial reshuffling following major crises such as the 2008 financial crisis. From a trade theory perspective, these findings support the Heckscher-Ohlin model's prediction of persistent specialization patterns based on factor endowments [@leamer1995heckscher], while challenging newer models that emphasize rapid industrial transformation through technology adoption [@grossman1993innovation; @helpman2025future]. The absence of significant restructuring in PageRank, betweenness, and eigenvector centralities indicates that core industries maintain their intermediary roles and influence positions within global supply chains, suggesting that established trade relationships create substantial switching costs and network externalities that preserve existing hierarchies even during periods of economic turbulence. As shown in Figure \ref{fig:top10sect}, industries with high centrality measures (such as agriculture financial services) also tend to exhibit high and growing value-added contributions. Nevertheless, the top 10 value added industries industries incorporate professional scientific and technical activities (M), public administration and defense (O), and human health and social works (Q) which are also selected in the calculation of the top 10 eigenvector-centralities. This correlation suggests that an industry's position in the trade network is often reflective of its economic importance in terms of value creation, which is further strengthened by similar industry characteristics in terms of both centrality and added value (compare Figures \ref{fig:top10sect}(b,g) with Figure \ref{fig:top10sect}(h)), as well as the high average correlation between \glspl{va} and the employed  out-strength ($\rho =$ `r round(mean(diag(cor(VAcent,t(var_sect_time[16,,])))),2)`) centrality values. 

However, the observed shifts in hub and authority centralities reveal more nuanced adjustments in industrial leadership and trust relationships within the global economy. Financial and insurance sector's declining hub centrality after 2011 -- overtaken by basic materials and construction -- reflects a fundamental reorientation of global economic priorities following the financial crisis, consistent with @reinhart2009time's and @kose2022aftermath's documentations of postcrisis shifts toward tangible asset sectors and infrastructure investment. This transition aligns with @rodrik2016premature's argument about "premature deindustrialization," where developing economies increasingly prioritize manufacturing and construction over financial services. The rise of basic materials in authority centrality suggests growing recognition of resource-rich countries and commodity-production industries as reliable trading partners, supporting @venables2016using's analysis of the "resource curse" reversal in countries that successfully leveraged commodity booms for broader economic development. These changes in authority reflect evolving trust patterns in international trade, where countries increasingly view suppliers of essential materials as more dependable than financial intermediaries -- a shift that has profound implications for supply chain resilience and strategic economic partnerships. The construction sector's emergence in authority centrality likely reflects the global infrastructure boom, particularly in emerging markets, consistent with the @world2017world's emphasis on infrastructure investment as a driver of sustainable development [@knack2025does].

According to Figure \ref{fig:sectpnda}, both the network indicators and \glspl{va} of industries can be clearly classified into 2-3 distinguishable clusters, which are similarly separated for most centrality and the \gls{va} measures, revealing fundamental economic stratification patterns that align with established theories of industrial organization and sectoral heterogeneity. The \gls{dco} and  \gls{ec} centralities characterizing the multiplicity of export partners show very similar patterns, and in the case of both centralities, two main characteristics whose trajectory after the 2008 financial crisis is completely different can be identified, demonstrating that these sector groupings exhibit distinct adaptive capacities in the wake of global disruptions. The results are also validated by clustering according to \gls{va}. We can see a similar sectoral breakdown, where the trends are the same as those seen with \gls{dco} and \gls{ec} centralities. This finding is consistent with @carvalho2014micro sectoral shock propagation theory, which suggests that industries with different network positions respond heterogeneously to aggregate shocks. Industries in the first cluster, such as agriculture, food products, and IT, demonstrate resilience and continue strengthening postcrisis, albeit at a slower pace, which economically reflects their essential nature and lower cyclical sensitivity, supporting @acemoglu2012network reported that upstream sectors and those providing basic necessities tends to be less volatile during economic downturns. These sectors are characterized by stronger integration and robust export partnerships, allowing them to sustain growth despite adverse conditions, which are consistent with @rauch2003starting and @roner2025survival evidence that differentiated product industries maintain more stable trade relationships. In contrast, industries in the second cluster, including mining, construction, and education, exhibit stagnation, potentially due to their higher cyclical sensitivity and dependence on domestic demand cycles, which aligns with @davis2001sectoral and @goswami2025job studies of procyclical employment patterns in construction and resource extraction sectors. The forecasts suggest expansion in export partnerships across both clusters, hinting at gradual recovery and broader network involvement, reflecting the economic principle of market adjustment through diversification strategies as described by @melitz2003impact. However, the predictions suggest convergence in homophily indicators between the two clusters, potentially reflecting ongoing structural transformation toward more integrated global production networks, supporting @baldwin2016great's concept of the "great convergence" in industrial structures. The significant decrease in modularity observed in the first cluster, while the concentration stagnates in the other clusters, economically suggests that leading industries are becoming more integrated into global markets while others remain relatively isolated, consistent with @autor2016china findings on the heterogeneous impacts of globalization across sectors. Decreasing betweenness centrality in the first cluster suggests that the intermediary role of these industries is weakening, while that of the second cluster, which includes several transport industries, is strengthening, reflecting a fundamental shift in the global division of labor where traditional manufacturing centers are being replaced by logistics and service hubs, supporting @gereffi2017global analysis of the global value chain governance transitions.

Economically, the complementary grouping tools clarify why specific sectors co-locate and how that maps into preparedness and policy design. Time-profile partitioning (\gls{gnda}; Figure \ref{fig:sectpnda}) reveals a fast-moving “input–coordination” constellation--farm and food systems, chemicals and advanced materials, semiconductors/electronics, freight and storage, digital infrastructure, and professional/technical services--whose joint motion arises from common choke-point inputs (e.g., fertilizers, rare earths, specialty chemicals, chips) and tight synchronization of logistics and data; actionable safeguards here include upstream buffer capacity for those inputs, narrowly scoped duty exemptions on bottleneck components, pre-cleared “green lanes” for cargo and data, and supplier spreads across at least three regions. A second, investment-sensitive “build-and-utilities” constellation--extraction and basic materials with building and energy/water services--clusters because capital-expenditure cycles bind them; counter-cyclical public orders, regional reserves of key materials, and rules-of-origin that reward dual sourcing dampen volatility. A slow-adjusting “social and knowledge” constellation--education, health, and cultural/publishing--moves together via income channels rather than input ties, calling for income smoothing and service-continuity contracts rather than border measures. Using multiple grouping lenses is essential: modularity-based partitions on indicator graphs highlight system levers; \gls{gnda} identifies who moves together and when; binary biclustering (iBBiG; Table \ref{tab:clustering_economic_interpretation}) pinpoints dense origin–target dyads that actually carry transmission. Overlaying lead–lag evidence from the causality tests onto these biclusters (Figure \ref{fig:caussect}) marks which dyads ignite cascades and the typical delay, enabling a tiered playbook: sentinel dashboards on the fast-moving constellations trigger narrow waivers and logistics fast-tracks; if the build-and-utilities constellation lights up next, deploy material swap lines and diversification mandates; if the slow constellation activates, pivot to demand-side stabilizers. This integrated reading turns otherwise technical groupings into precise, time-sequenced resilience and trade actions.

The observed temporal differentiation in industrial responsiveness patterns reflects fundamental economic structural characteristics that determine adjustment speeds to global trade disruptions. Early-responding industries--primarily agriculture and food products (A01_02), electronics (C26), financial services (K), and telecommunications (J61)--exhibit characteristics associated with rapid market adjustment capabilities: high technology intensity, short production cycles, and immediate consumer demand sensitivity [@acemoglu2012competing; @autor2020fall]. These sectors typically operate with lower capital intensity and higher labor mobility, enabling swift reallocation of resources during economic shocks, consistent with @melitz2014heterogeneous findings on firm heterogeneity in trade adjustment. The early responsiveness of the electronics sector aligns with @timmer2014slicing's and @kordalska2025decoding's studies of rapid global value chain reconfiguration in technology-intensive industries, where modular production processes facilitate quick supplier switching and geographic relocation. Conversely, late-responding industries--construction (F), basic materials (C24), and utilities (D, E)--are characterized by high capital intensity, long investment horizons, and substantial sunk costs that create adjustment rigidities [@decker2020changing]. These upstream and midstream industries face structural constraints including long-term contracts, specialized infrastructure, and regulatory frameworks that impede rapid reconfiguration, supporting @antras2013organizing theory of sequential production and adjustment costs in global supply chains. The intermediate timing of manufacturing industries (C20, C28, C29) reflects their position in value chains where adjustment speeds depend on both upstream input availability and downstream demand patterns, creating moderate response lags that correspond to inventory cycles and production planning horizons [@alfaro2019internalizing]. This sectoral stratification suggests that trade policy interventions should be temporally sequenced: immediate support for technology-intensive and service sectors, medium-term assistance for manufacturing, and long-term structural programs for capital-intensive industries, recognizing that cross-country variations within the same industry may reflect differences in technological sophistication, market structure, and institutional frameworks [@caselli2020diversification; @conteduca2025trade].

This temporal granularity is invisible to traditional industrial classification systems but crucial for policy timing.-->

These results indicate that the systematic lag between the initial disruptions and their broader economic consequences. While changes in homophily (as an indication of a change in the industry trade structure) and centrality indicators (as an indication of the changed role of industries) emerges early in sectors such as computing, electronics, finance, and telecommunications, cascading effects reach industries such as education, social work, publishing, and construction much later. This delayed response underscores how crises often unfold in waves, first impacting direct trade and financial hubs and then trickling down to peripheral sectors. If a crisis escalates, then industries dependent on discretionary spending, such as arts, entertainment, and recreation, will likely suffer the most prolonged instability. Ultimately, these patterns emphasize the importance of proactive policy measures and diversified trade strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities across industrial sectors, ensuring resilience in the face of global economic upheavals.

## Reorganization of Countries' Positions in International Trade

The primary takeaway from Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry} is that the global dominance of leading countries is declining, while leadership roles are being significantly rearranged (compare Figures \ref{fig:top10ctry}(a-g) to Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(h)). The results are illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry} underscore the changing dynamics of global trade networks, particularly the rising significance of dominating states, especially China. During the examined timeframe, China's rise is characterized by a steady growth in export quantities, centrality metrics across all sectors (see Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(b,d-f)), and \glspl{fd} (see Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(h)), in stark contrast to the declining relative centrality values of other prominent countries. This trend highlights China's strategic emphasis on augmenting its involvement in commerce and supply chains (see Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(d-e)), establishing itself as a pivotal mediator of global trade. The shift in dominance from the US to China, as indicated by metrics such as PageRank (see Figure \ref{fig:top10ctry}(b)), hub (d), authority centralities (e), and \glspl{fd} (h), signifies a significant reconfiguration of trade relations and underscore China's increasing power and essential role in global supply chains. The present Trump administration's China policy appears to be a rational measure; nonetheless, importantly, owing to global interconnection, the ramifications of the tariff conflict extend beyond China and may negatively influence the entire trade framework.

The observed grouping of countries' trade based on Granger causality analysis highlights the temporal dynamics of trade interactions, suggesting underlying economic interdependencies and responsiveness among nations. The first group, which includes Estonia, the United Kingdom, and several Asian countries, indicates that these economies are quick to respond to shifts in trade, owing to their export-driven growth strategies and integration in global supply chains. The subsequent grouping, emerging after an average of `r round(year12,2)` years, encompasses a more diverse array of countries, suggesting a broader economic network that reacts to initial changes in trade by adapting their exports and imports accordingly, reflecting the interconnectedness of global trade flows. The notable lag of `r round(year23,2)` years for the third group underscores the delayed response of larger, often more established economies such as the US and Germany, which may be less agile owing to their size and complexity but significant in world trade dynamics. The observed causal relationships between the two middle groups, with an average lag of `r round(year32,2)` years from the countries in the third group, suggests that if changes do occur in the third group, then they will also affect countries in the second group, as is likely the case with the current US--Europe tariffs. Finally, Sweden and Ukraine belong to the group of late responders, which suggests that the effects of potential crises appear the latest here or that they are able to adequately mitigate their effects. These findings emphasize the intricate and varied nature of global trade interactions, highlighting the importance of considering temporal dynamics in economic analyses to better understand the causal relationships among countries in terms of trade.

Ultimately, the causality of industry shifts and trade transformations is intrinsically linked. Early-reacting countries are home to industry that are the first to undergo structural changes, reinforcing the idea that economic shocks propagate through industrial sectors before expanding to national trade policies. As trade adjustments appear to follow cascading patterns -- with an initial group reacting first, which is followed by broader economic shifts --; thus, it becomes crucial for policymakers and businesses to anticipate disruptions on the basis of industrial vulnerabilities.
